note.note:
Action Plan:
1. Assess and monitor for airway compromise after insect sting — patient observed remotely and judged not to have life‑threatening airway involvement at time of consult; patient advised to go to A&E immediately if breathing worsens, if they develop stridor, marked lip/tongue swelling, or other signs of anaphylaxis.
2. Treat current symptoms with oral antihistamine: advised Piriton (chlorphenamine) 4 mg — one tablet; may be repeated up to six times daily as needed. (Doctor also offered an unspecified "one‑a‑day" antihistamine option — dose/route/frequency not documented.)
3. Monitor local sting site for signs of spreading infection (increasing redness, warmth, spreading erythema, fever); if those signs develop, contact clinician — antibiotics may be considered.
4. No immediate allergy testing or epinephrine recommended given current exam; if recurrent reactions occur consider referral for allergy testing later.
5. Provide patient education about anaphylaxis signs and when to seek urgent care; clinician will leave a link to information for patient review.
6. Safety net / follow up: return to A&E for acute deterioration, or contact primary care / this service if concerned or symptoms persist/worsen. Lower threshold for contact if anxious.
7. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
- Reason for visit: Acute difficulty breathing and subjective lip/tongue swelling shortly after an insect sting (bee/wasp) a few minutes prior to consultation.
- Onset/duration/progression: Sting occurred “just a few minutes ago.” Patient reports subjective shortness of breath (not acutely worsening) and odd sensation/possible slight swelling of right-sided lip and tongue. Anxiety about possible progression.
- Local findings reported: Puncture mark on right arm with mild redness/blotchy rash; described as slightly sore; no marked swelling reported by patient.
- Past medical history: Eczema.
- Allergies: Penicillin allergy reported.
- Medications: No regular medications reported; no antihistamine or epinephrine taken prior to consult.
- Social history: Lives alone; works as a computer scientist; has a pet cat.
- Psychiatric history: Occasional anxiety; no prior medication for anxiety.
- Prior severe allergic reactions: Patient reports no history of anaphylaxis and has never been prescribed an EpiPen.

Objective:
- General appearance/airway/respiratory (remote video exam):
  - Patient speaking normally; clinician reports breathing appears non‑labored.
  - No audible stridor reported.
  - No visible lip or oropharyngeal swelling on inspection; throat visualized and no edema noted.
- Local exam (remote): Right arm puncture mark visible with mild redness/blotchy rash; clinician did not observe significant swelling or warmth.
- Vitals/investigations: None documented in transcript.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Insect sting allergic reaction (possible large local reaction vs early/an evolving anaphylaxis):
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Large local allergic reaction (condition name only). Supported by DDx: "Large local allergic reaction (localized urticaria/inflammatory reaction to insect sting)" — likelihood: High (DDx).
   - Differential diagnosis (DDx items consistent with transcript):
     - Early/evolving IgE‑mediated anaphylaxis — likelihood: Medium (DDx). 
       - Supporting evidence: Symptoms began minutes after sting; patient reports subjective dyspnea and lip/tongue oddness.
       - Opposing evidence: Clinician observed normal breathing, clear speech, no stridor or visible oropharyngeal swelling; no hypotension or systemic features documented.
     - Anxiety / panic‑related dyspnea — likelihood: Medium (DDx).
       - Supporting evidence: Patient endorses occasional anxiety; clinician noted anxiety contributing to concern; objective exam reassuring.
   - Investigations planned: None at time of consult; no blood tests or imaging indicated currently.
   - Treatment planned:
     - Oral antihistamine recommended: chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg — one tablet, may be repeated up to 6 times/day as needed.
     - Alternate option offered: “one‑a‑day” antihistamine (agent and dose not documented).
     - Safety net: Immediate presentation to A&E if breathing worsens, stridor develops, marked lip/tongue swelling occurs, or other signs of anaphylaxis.
   - Referrals: None acutely. Consider allergy referral/testing only if recurrent reactions occur (clinician advised this is not required now).

2. Local skin reaction at sting site / risk of secondary infection:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Local inflammatory reaction (condition name only). Supported by DDx: "Large local allergic reaction / local tissue trauma" — likelihood: High for local reaction; "local bacterial cellulitis" — likelihood: Low (DDx).
   - Differential diagnosis (from DDx consistent with transcript):
     - Local bacterial cellulitis — likelihood: Low.
       - Supporting evidence: Local erythema and soreness present.
       - Opposing evidence: Onset within minutes of sting (bacterial cellulitis usually develops over hours–days); no warmth, spreading redness, systemic signs documented.
   - Investigations planned: None immediately.
   - Treatment planned:
     - Conservative local care and monitoring.
     - If redness spreads, becomes hot, more painful, or systemic features develop — clinician may consider starting antibiotics and reassessment.
   - Referrals: None acute.

3. Anxiety related to reaction and concern about progression:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Anxiety/panic‑related symptoms (condition name only). Supported by DDx: "Anxiety/panic attack" — likelihood: Medium (DDx).
   - Differential diagnosis: Primary physiological allergic reaction vs anxiety as contributory factor (both discussed).
   - Investigations planned: None.
   - Treatment planned:
     - Reassurance provided, education on signs of anaphylaxis.
     - Encouraged lower threshold for contacting service if anxious; clinician offered that a chat can help calm concerns.
   - Referrals: None acute; consider mental health support if anxiety becomes frequent/significant (not indicated at present).

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - No vital signs documented (heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature).
  - No exact name/dose for the "one‑a‑day" antihistamine option (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - No documentation re: availability/prescription of intramuscular epinephrine (EpiPen) in case of future reactions.
  - No medication reconciliation (current regular medications list absent).
  - No time stamps for events beyond “a few minutes ago.”
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None significant; DDx includes broader rare diagnoses (pulmonary embolism, laryngeal neoplasm, hereditary angioedema) that are low probability and were not advocated by clinician — no direct conflict noted. (conflict noted: none)
- Transcript quality: Good audio/video quality evident; clinician was able to visually inspect mouth and arm; no significant inaudible sections.
